IndusEquip Corp - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusEquip Corp Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star then 1 on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then 2. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusEquip Corp's results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; David Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusEquip Corp's performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, navigating a challenging macroeconomic landscape while executing on our strategic priorities. We've seen solid order intake despite headwinds, with our book-to-bill ratio holding strong at 1.15 times, and we've continued to shorten lead times across key product lines, reflecting improved supply chain resilience. Operating margins expanded meaningfully across most segments, driven by favorable mix and cost discipline, even as we've managed elevated inventory levels effectively. Supply chain constraints have eased somewhat, allowing us to maintain high on-time delivery rates. Overall, these factors have positioned us well, with a robust backlog providing clear visibility.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Chen to provide more detail on our financial results.

David Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Michael. Turning to our financial performance, IndusEquip Corp reported $1.72 billion in revenue for the third quarter, representing a 10% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 38.2%, driven by pricing discipline averaging 4.5% pass-through and a favorable shift toward higher-margin automation products. Operating expenses were $552 million, resulting in an operating income of $250 million. Our net income for the quarter was $190 million, or $1.85 adjusted earnings per share, up 8% from the prior year.

We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue of $6.8 to $7.0 billion, reflecting 2-4% organic growth, and adjusted EPS of $7.20 to $7.50. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through our ongoing $500 million share repurchase program and maintaining our dividend at a sustainable 2.5 times net debt to EBITDA ratio.

As we dive deeper, I'd like to address the impact of macroeconomic factors on end-market demand, which has been the dominant theme shaping our visibility this quarter. While we've delivered this solid performance, the macro environment remains choppy, particularly in our core segments of metalworking, automation systems, and material handling equipment.

Let me break it down systematically, starting with the key macroeconomic drivers influencing our customers' capital expenditure decisions. Elevated interest rates continue to weigh heavily on capex cycles. With the Fed's terminal rate around 5.25-5.50%, corporate borrowing costs have risen by 200-250 basis points since early 2022, leading to widespread deferrals in non-critical projects. In our industrial OEM end-market, which represents 35% of our revenue, order intake softened by 7% sequentially, aligning with the ISM Manufacturing PMI's contractionary reading of 47.8 in September. Customers such as tier-1 suppliers to Ford and GM are prioritizing inventory destocking and free cash flow preservation over new CNC machining centers or robotic welding lines, much like Caterpillar's recent report of a 10% drop in resource industries orders.

Inflation dynamics add another layer of complexity. Core PPI for industrial machinery held steady at 3.2% year-over-year, but persistent wage pressures and commodity volatility—with steel up 12% in Q3 due to supply constraints from the Ukraine conflict—have squeezed customer margins. This has resulted in elongated sales cycles, now averaging 120 days compared to our historical 90-day norm, especially for high-precision 5-axis mills used in aerospace. On a positive note, our pricing discipline has maintained gross margins at 38.2%, though demand elasticity is clear: every 1% rise in U.S. 10-year Treasury yields correlates to a 2-3% pullback in our discretionary capex orders, per our internal econometric modeling.

Shifting to sector-specific trends, the semiconductor end-market has been a bright spot, supported by the CHIPS Act and AI-driven capex. Global fab equipment spending is projected to reach $120 billion in 2024 according to SEMI data, driving 22% year-over-year growth in our cleanroom automation systems. Orders from TSMC and Intel partners surged 18% quarter-over-quarter, fueled by demand for our vacuum handling robots optimized for 2nm node processes. In contrast, the automotive sector, 25% of our mix, faced headwinds from softening EV demand amid high financing rates—U.S. EV sales growth slowed to 4% year-over-year per Cox Automotive. This delayed orders for our battery assembly lines by 15%, similar to Deere & Co.'s commentary on production equipment weakness.

Regionally, the outlook is mixed. North America, accounting for 45% of revenue, saw industrial production rise modestly 1.2% year-over-year per Fed data, aided by reshoring under the IRA. Our U.S. backlog grew 12% to $2.8 billion, with strength in renewables—wind turbine component machining up 25% as Vestas and GE Vernova ramp domestic supply chains. Europe, at 30% of sales, declined 5% in demand, impacted by the ECB's restrictive policy and energy costs 20% above pre-Ukraine levels. German machine tool orders fell 8% per VDW association stats, affecting our hydraulic press brake sales to OEMs like Volkswagen. China, with 15% exposure, stabilized after the property crisis but grew only 3% in fixed asset investment; our Shanghai JV localization strategy delivered 10% order growth in EV battery gigafactories, offsetting softness in heavy machinery. Emerging markets like Mexico and India offered tailwinds, with maquiladora capex up 14% on nearshoring, boosting material handling palletizers.

Strategically, we're countering these pressures by accelerating our digital thread platform, IndusLink 4.0, which integrates IoT sensors and AI predictive maintenance—piloted with Boeing for aerospace spindles, reducing downtime 30% and unlocking $150 million in aftermarket services potential. Diversification into high-growth verticals like life sciences and data centers now makes up 20% of our pipeline, up from 12% last year.

Looking ahead, we anticipate Q4 orders stabilizing with PMI at 49, and potential Fed cuts in H1 2025 catalyzing a capex rebound. Visibility is strong with a $4.2 billion backlog covering nine months of production, supporting our FY24 revenue guide.

Next, let's discuss operating margin performance by segment. Consolidated operating margins expanded 170 basis points year-over-year to 14.5%, our strongest since pre-pandemic levels. This was powered by a favorable product mix toward higher-margin automation and aftermarket services, disciplined pricing, and $85 million in structural cost savings from our Enterprise Lean Sigma program and supply chain optimization.

In Machinery & Automation, 32% of revenue, margins rose to 16.2% from 14.5%—a 170 basis point gain. Volume grew 12% year-over-year on demand for next-gen CNC machining centers and collaborative robotic arms, with 4.2% pricing realization passing through steel and aluminum inflation. Digital twin technology across 15 production lines in Rockford, Illinois, uplifted margins 220 basis points via predictive maintenance and 18% scrap reduction. North America, 55% of segment revenue, hit 17.8% margins on IIJA infrastructure spending; APAC was 13.9% softer due to China's semiconductor slowdown, offset by Chennai production ramps. We're prioritizing Industry 4.0 edge AI to gain share in the $120 billion global automation market from Fanuc and ABB.

Heavy Equipment, 28% of revenue, saw margins contract 140 basis points to 11.8% on mix headwinds from lower-margin mining loaders despite 8% revenue growth from 6% volume and 2% pricing. Input inflation in Tier 4 Final diesel engines and rubber tracks pressured gross margins 90 basis points, akin to Caterpillar's commodity volatility. EMEA held at 12.5% on EU Green Deal rail projects; LatAm dipped to 9.2% from Brazil iron ore slowdowns. Cost actions like 15% workforce optimization in Peoria and supplier consolidation added 110 basis points. We're advancing hydrogen-ready dozers for 15%+ margins by 2025.

Precision Components, 22% of revenue, expanded 140 basis points to 18.5% on a rich mix—25% up in aero parts like turbine blades amid Boeing and Airbus ramps. Revenues rose 14% organically, pricing up 3% on alloys. Additive manufacturing with laser powder bed fusion cut lead times 40% at Wichita, adding 160 basis points. North America drove 65% growth at 20.1%; APAC steady at 16.8%. Vertical integration from melt to machine de-risks supply versus Howmet Aerospace peers. A $50 million composites center targets eVTOL and hypersonics.

Aftermarket Services, 18% of revenue, held 28.4% margins—up 50 basis points sequentially on 16% recurring growth from IoT uptime contracts at 72% attachment. Labor productivity gained 9% via AR field service, like Honeywell Forge. North America 29.2%, EMEA 27.8% on wind services, APAC 28.1%. This segment is 45% of operating profit, shifting to asset-light recurring models like Deere's precision ag.

In summary, segment margins show execution amid dynamics: easing frictions, $200 million German laser cutter acquisition, sustainability products for IRA credits. Full-year at high end of 13-14% guidance, Q4 from aftermarket and wins.

Turning to supply chain constraints and component availability, we've advanced resilience amid Red Sea delays, semiconductor shortages, and raw material volatility, delivering 18% revenue growth and 92% on-time delivery for G-Series CNC centers and HydraLift presses.

Lead times for critical components averaged 18 weeks entering the quarter, down from 28 weeks peak. Dual-sourcing shifted 35% Tier 1 semiconductors from Asia to U.S., Taiwan, Malaysia; MCUs for robotic welders hit 95% fill rates from 72%, clearing 15% automation backlog.

Steel and forgings, 28% BOM, spiked 12% on mill curtailments and energy surcharges, but forward contracts with Nucor and ArcelorMittal lock 8% below spot, stabilizing COGS at 41.2%. Electromechanicals like Siemens/ABB servo motors and VFDs dropped 22% to 12 weeks via $150 million inventory build, now 14 weeks coverage at 4.2x turns above ISM 3.8x.

North America, 55% revenue, robust at 65% domestic content via "Forge Local"; 40% bearings nearshored to Mexico SKF. EMEA at 20 weeks challenged by strikes, but Dublin hub boosts 88% fill for Volkswagen grinding. Asia-Pacific gains: China electronics down to 28% from 45%, Vietnam/India cuts 30% lead times, +150 bps margins on freight.

Our Supply Chain Digital Twin with SAP Ariba and Palantir offers 98% traceability across 2,500 suppliers, cutting forecast variance 25% for rare earth hedging. Vertical pilots: 51% Ohio hydraulic stake for 20% self-sufficiency; $80 million Mexico VFD line. Ahead of Caterpillar's backlog slips and Ingersoll Rand semis.

Expect 14-16 weeks year-end, 94% delivery; +200 bps margins on drawdowns, monitoring tariffs. $2.3 billion backlog up 12% reflects confidence in eForge batteries.

Finally, on inventory levels and management strategies, consolidated inventory ended Q3 at $1.2 billion, down 2% sequentially and 5% year-over-year. DIO at 82 days versus 88 last year and ISM 95 benchmark; turns at 4.5x from 4.1x, with 96% on-time delivery competing with Haas and DMG Mori.

Destocking since mid-2022 'bullwhip' trimmed raw materials 8% QoQ to $504 million on normalized steel/aluminum via Nucor/Alcoa hedging. WIP $336 million gained from ERP MRP cycle cuts in Ohio/Monterrey. Finished goods $360 million trimmed 4% on promotions ahead of HyperForce cobot launch.

North America 75 DIO for reshoring like Intel Ohio/GM EV; Europe 95 DIO mitigated by Bosch Rexroth VMI; APAC $240 million build at 4.8x turns for semis.

ABC/XYZ segmentation: AI demand sensing on SAP S/4HANA for A-items cuts stockouts 25%, overstock 15%. Supplier scorecards with Timken/Siemens enforce 98% delivery via blockchain post-Red Sea. Digital twins with ML on PMI/steel futures hit 92% accuracy.

Guide 3-5% Q4 reduction to 78-80 DIO, 95%+ fill. Multi-sourcing derisks China dumping; flex for capex upside. Fuels 90%+ FCF, outpacing Caterpillar.

Now, I'll hand over to Lisa Patel, COO, for an operational update.

Lisa Patel (COO):
Thank you, David. Operationally, we've streamlined our supply chain and boosted manufacturing efficiency through new initiatives yielding results. Complementing David's points on lead times, our company-wide average for core products like heavy-duty excavators, CNC centers, and gas turbine assemblies stood at 22 weeks end-Q3, down 27% year-over-year from 30 weeks and from 25 weeks prior quarter—ahead of Caterpillar and Komatsu mid-20s. High-volume components like hydraulic cylinders, steel forgings, and PLC controls averaged 10 weeks, down 20%.

Construction Equipment compressed to 18 weeks from 26 via kanban with Nucor/Steel Dynamics. Power Systems at 16 weeks on nickel alloy stocking despite Russia issues. Semis for servo drives/IoT kits at 11 weeks, 31% better via CHIPS Act fabs. Raw materials 7 weeks on hedging.

North America normalized at 20 weeks, accelerating conversions 15%; Europe 28 weeks eased by Leipzig hub; Asia 24 weeks offset by Vietnam ramp targeting sub-20. Investments: $150 million vertical integration in Alabama for 40% steel; SAP S/4HANA AI forecasting at 92% accuracy; digital twins cut prototyping 35%. Mexico expansion 25% for nearshoring. Book-to-bill 1.25x, backlog $4.2 billion up 18%; guide 19 weeks year-end for 200 bps EBITDA.

We're monitoring global chains proactively, investing in automation and digital tech to enhance capabilities.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then 1. Our first question comes from John Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

John Smith (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

David Chen:
Good morning, John. Rising raw material costs, particularly steel up 12% in Q3 from Ukraine constraints and commodity volatility, have pressured margins but we've offset through forward contracting below spot with Nucor and ArcelorMittal, stabilizing COGS at 41.2%. Pricing actions of 4.2-4.5% across segments, mix shifts to automation, and cost savings like Enterprise Lean Sigma $85 million have driven 170 bps operating margin expansion to 14.5%. Inventory buffers and hedging 60% exposure keep us resilient, with gross margins steady at 38.2% despite inflation mirroring Caterpillar's experience.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis (Goldman Sachs):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

Michael Reynolds:
Thanks, Emily. Aftermarket remains a high-margin cornerstone at 28.4% operating margins, 18% of revenue, with 16% recurring growth from IoT uptime contracts at 72% attachment rates. Uptime via predictive analytics and AR field service drove 9% productivity gains, balanced regionally: North America 29.2%, EMEA 27.8% on wind expansions, APAC 28.1%. It's 45% of operating profit now, shifting to recurring models. Outlook strong with digital thread like IndusLink 4.0 unlocking $150 million upside, seasonal Q4 strength, and megatrends in automation where book-to-bill exceeds 1.3x.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Robert Lee (Barclays):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

Lisa Patel:
Absolutely, Robert. As I noted, we've made strong headway: 22 weeks company-wide for excavators, CNC, turbines—27% YoY reduction ahead of peers. Components at 10 weeks. Construction to 18 weeks on kanban; power systems 16 weeks; semis 11 weeks via multi-sourcing and CHIPS. Regional normalization: North America 20 weeks, Europe down 4 via hubs, Asia targeting sub-20 with Vietnam. Drivers include $150 million vertical integration, 92% forecast accuracy on SAP AI, digital twins. Guide to 19 weeks year-end, boosting margins 200 bps and book-to-bill to 1.25x on $4.2 billion backlog.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions and your interest in IndusEquip Corp. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
